bridge: Builds on B02 parameter binding, W01 request evidence and S06 ownership. Use SQLite in memory or the designated SQL injection labs; do not target a real website.
teaching:
SQL injection occurs when untrusted data changes query structure. Quoting by hand is fragile because the correct interpretation depends on the database and context. Parameter binding gives the database query structure and values through separate API channels.

The repair must preserve intended behaviour. A function that rejects every name avoids the attack but breaks valid users; include valid and invalid cases. Dynamic sort columns cannot generally be bound as values, so choose them from a fixed allowlist and keep the query syntax controlled.

A secure query still needs authorisation. Selecting by note id with a bound parameter prevents syntax injection but can still expose another owner's row. Use both parameterisation and the intended ownership predicate. Avoid treating one vulnerability class as proof of complete endpoint security.
example:
import sqlite3
c=sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
c.execute("CREATE TABLE notes(id INTEGER, owner TEXT, body TEXT)")
c.executemany("INSERT INTO notes VALUES(?,?,?)",[(1,"A","one"),(2,"B","two")])
def read_note(caller,note_id):
    return c.execute("SELECT body FROM notes WHERE id=? AND owner=?",(note_id,caller)).fetchall()
print(read_note("A",1))  # [('one',)]
print(read_note("A",2))  # []
explanation: The fixed statement constrains both object and owner. caller must come from verified identity in a real service. Binding an integer-looking string is still data binding; it should not create a new SQL clause. Input schema validation may additionally reject an unexpected type.
exercise: Run this exact fixture. Test A/1, A/2, B/2, B/99 and an id value of the harmless literal text 1 OR 1=1. Record returned rows and explain the separation between syntax safety and ownership.
solution: Only A/1 and B/2 return their own body. Missing/foreign objects return no rows; the expression-like string remains data rather than becoming SQL logic. A real integer-only schema may reject it before querying.
challenge: Design safe filtering by owner plus a user-selected sort key chosen from id or body. State how unsupported sort keys are handled and why a placeholder is not a general SQL identifier mechanism.
challenge_solution: Use a fixed map {id: trusted-id-fragment, body: trusted-body-fragment}; reject other choices. Bind owner values separately. Include valid sort behaviour and unsupported-key rejection in tests.
